confounds: The development corpus has a fixed label composition of 618 diagnosed and 5464 control users, approximately 10.2% diagnosed; classifier thresholds and positive predictive value depend on the unseen deployment prior.
All users have at least 50 retained posts, so the corpus is conditioned on activity and cannot support absence-of-posts interpretations.
Diagnosed users are more prolific, and raw post counts can be dominated by a few high-volume users.
Source order is available but timestamps are not; duration, onset, and true temporal persistence cannot be established.
Mental-health vocabulary is heavily confounded by replies, reposts, quotation, third-person talk, music/film/news, advocacy, jokes, bereavement, physical illness, and temporary situational distress.
Stable sexuality, school-age, fandom, and online-discourse differences indicate demographic or collection artifacts that can masquerade as clinical signal.
Hashtags are absent and several punctuation/style features are nearly universal, suggesting preprocessing or platform-specific collection artifacts.

caveats: Activity may reflect platform engagement, age, recruitment, or selection rather than symptoms.
No held-out-fold prior or collection mechanism may be inferred.
findings.evidence_summary: Diagnosed users have longer retained timelines, so pooled post counts can overstate lexical differences. All users have at least 50 retained posts, indicating collection conditioning.
findings.prompt_guidance: Normalize by user and include log timeline size; prefer user prevalence and per-user rates over pooled post totals.

findings.signal: Diagnosed timelines without broad clinical vocabulary

negative_results: Generic hopelessness/frustration vocabulary is near-saturated and unstable: 92.9% diagnosed versus 90.3% control users overall, with the direction reversing in fold 2.
Raw depression-term frequency is collection-sensitive: control users averaged 1.24 matching posts in fold 0 versus 0.72 for diagnosed users, while folds 1–3 reversed this pattern.
Positive-affect and social-support language are not absent from diagnosed timelines: prevalence is 99.8% versus 97.5% and 100.0% versus 98.4%, respectively.
Hashtags were absent, while question marks, short posts, long posts, and capitalization were nearly ubiquitous; these are uninformative features.
